'''Kyle F. Anderson''' (born September 20, 1993)<ref name=uclabio/> is an American [[basketball]] player who recently completed his college career for the [[UCLA Bruins men's basketball|UCLA Bruins]]. In his sophomore year in 2013–14, he was an [[List of All-Pacific-12 Conference men's basketball teams|all-conference]] player in the [[Pacific-12 Conference]] and earned [[NCAA Men's Basketball All-Americans|All-American]] honors.

Anderson developed the ball-handling skills of a [[point guard]] at an early age, but his height provided him the versatility to play as a [[forward (basketball)|forward]]. As a high school player in [[New Jersey]], Anderson led his teams to two consecutive state titles, and was named state player of the year during his senior year. One of the top recruits out of high school, Anderson was named All-Pac-12 second team while playing mostly at forward in his freshman year with UCLA. The following season, he moved to point guard, and was voted the Most Outstanding Player of the [[Pacific-12 Conference Men's Basketball Tournament|Pac-12 Tournament]] as the Bruins won their first conference tournament title in six years.

==Early life==
Anderson was born in [[New York City]], and grew up in [[Fairview, New Jersey]].<ref name=uclabio/> He started playing basketball the day he started walking, which was three days before his first birthday. He attended his first basketball camp at age three.<ref name=parker/> Anderson's father, a longtime high school basketball coach in New Jersey, groomed him to be a [[point guard]]. Although Anderson was tall, his father did not want him to be "pigeonholed" as a [[post (basketball)|post]] player.<ref name=foster_03122014>{{cite news|last=Foster|first=Chris|title=UCLA's Kyle Anderson doesn't lack confidence or intensity|date=March 12, 2014|newspaper=Los Angeles Times|url=http://www.latimes.com/sports/college/ucla/la-sp-ucla-kyle-anderson-20140313,0,6102973,full.story#axzz2wAciTPAt|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/6O7ynGQRN|archivedate=March 16, 2014|deadurl=no}}</ref> He had his son play with older players on [[Amateur Athletic Union]] (AAU) teams; usually the smallest player on the court, Anderson developed point guard skills early while passing to his larger teammates.<ref name=parker>{{cite news|last=Parker|first=Brandon|title=St. Anthony's Kyle Anderson takes winning to a different level|date=November 14, 2011|work=ESPN.com|url=http://espn.go.com/blog/high-school/new-jersey/post/_/id/486/st-anthonys-kyle-anderson-takes-winning-to-a-different-level|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/6NXyRvcOV|archivedate=February 21, 2014|deadurl=no}}</ref><ref name=hamilton_01092014/>

He began his high school career at [[Paterson Catholic High School]].  Although he possessed the skills of a point guard, his {{convert|6|ft|5|in|m|adj=on}} height led coaches to play him on the wing or in the post. After two years at Paterson Catholic, the school closed, and Anderson moved to [[St. Anthony High School (New Jersey)|St. Anthony High School]].<ref name=parker/> Overall, he compiled 119–6 record as a four-year starter, including 65–0 in his two years at St. Anthony.<ref name=haley_09162012/> When St. Anthony captured its second straight [[Tournament of Champions (NJSIAA)|New Jersey Tournament of Champions]] title and concluded its second straight undefeated season with a 66–62 victory over Plainfield, Anderson was the team’s third-leading scorer with 14 [[point (basketball)|points]]. Still, St. Anthony coach [[Bob Hurley]] said Anderson was the team's "heart and soul and he was the reason we won the game.’’<ref name=haley_09162012>{{cite news|url=http://www.nj.com/hssports/blog/boysbasketball/index.ssf/2012/04/kyle_anderson_of_st_anthony_is_the_star-ledgers_state_boys_basketball_player_of_the_year_for_2011-12.html|title=Kyle Anderson of St. Anthony is The Star-Ledger's state boys basketball Player of the Year for 2011–12|newspaper=The Star-Ledger|accessdate=September 16, 2012|date=April 1, 2013|first=John|last=Haley}}</ref> For the season, Anderson led the team in scoring (14.7 points per game), [[rebound (basketball)|rebounding]] (6.5 per game), [[assist (basketball)|assists]] (3.9 per game), [[block (basketball)|blocked shots]] (2.0 per game) and deflections. ''[[The Star-Ledger]]'' named him their state boys basketball Player of the Year.<ref name=haley_09162012/> He received national recognition as a ''[[Parade (magazine)|Parade]]'' All-American, [[McDonald's All-American Game|McDonald's All-American]], and he was invited to play in the [[Jordan Brand Classic]] and [[Nike Hoop Summit]].<ref name=uclabio/> In spite of all the praise he had received in his career, Anderson was described by Hurley as "unassuming", which the coach credited to Anderson's family doing a "great job keeping him balanced."<ref name=haley_09162012/>

The {{convert|6|ft|8|in|m|adj=on}} Anderson was often listed as a [[small forward]],<ref name=telep_09192011/><ref>{{cite news|last=Stanmyre|first=Matthew|title=St. Anthony star Kyle Anderson stayed poised during recruiting process before choosing UCLA|date=September 21, 2011|newspaper=The Star-Ledger|url=http://www.nj.com/setonhall/index.ssf/2011/09/st_anthony_star_kyle_anderson.html|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/6NY4F5yHH|archivedate=February 21, 2014|deadurl=no}}</ref> but still considered himself a point guard.<ref>{{cite news|last=DeCourcy|first=Mike|title=Point guard Dominic Artis decommits from UCLA|date=October 6, 2011|work=SportingNews.com|url=http://www.sportingnews.com/ncaa-basketball/story/2011-10-06/point-guard-dominic-artis-decommits-from-ucla|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/6NY3HzBpg|archivedate=February 21, 2011|deadurl=no}}</ref> Among 2012 recruits, he was ranked the No. 1 small forward by [[Rivals.com]], and No. 2 by [[ESPN.com]] and [[Scout.com]] behind [[Shabazz Muhammad]].<ref name=uclabio>{{cite web|title=Kyle Anderson Biography|work=UCLABruins.com|url=http://www.uclabruins.com/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_OEM_ID=30500&ATCLID=207913795|accessdate=February 21, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://rivals.yahoo.com/basketballrecruiting/basketball/recruiting/player-Kyle-Anderson-87009|title=KYLE ANDERSON|accessdate=September 16, 2012|date=|publisher=Rivals|author=}}</ref> Hurley called Anderson's passing "his best asset."<ref name=haley_09162012/>

==International play==
Anderson participated in U16 and U17 training camps for [[USA Basketball]] prior to being named to the 2009–10 [[USA Basketball Men's Developmental National Team]].<ref name=halley_03062012>{{cite news|last=Halley|first=Jim|title=USA Basketball names 10 players to Nike Hoop Summit team|date=March 6, 2012|newspaper=USA Today|url=http://usatoday30.usatoday.com/sports/preps/basketball/story/2012-03-06/Nike-Hoop-Summit-names-US-roster/53388858/1|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/6OB2DDKkJ|archivedate=March 18, 2014|deadurl=no}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.usabasketball.com/bios/anderson_kyle.html|title=USA Basketball: Kyle Anderson|date=|publisher=USA Basketball|author=|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/6OB2GL0h7|archivedate=March 18, 2014}}</ref> In 2012, he started at power forward for the [[USA Basketball Junior National Select Team]] that competed at the [[Nike Hoop Summit]], which featured the top American high school seniors against a team of international players aged 19 or younger.<ref name=halley_03062012/><ref>{{cite news|last=Shoals|first=Bethlehem|title=Nike Hoop Summit 2012 Recap|date=April 9, 2012|work=slamonline.com|url=http://www.slamonline.com/online/college-hs/high-school/2012/04/nike-hoop-summit-2012-recap/|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/6OB2xvv1s|archivedate=March 18, 2014|deadurl=no}}</ref>

==Player profile==
[[File:Kyle Anderson drives vs Oregon.JPG|thumb|upright|240px|Anderson nicknamed "Slow Mo" after his deliberate style]]
Out of high school, Anderson was considered capable of playing any of four positions on the court, from point guard to power forward, drawing comparisons to basketball legends [[Magic Johnson]] and [[Larry Bird]]. Anderson's high school coach [[Bobby Hurley]] said, "I think he's a modern-day Magic Johnson. I think that let him play the point. He gets everybody shots. You don’t have him back defensively balancing the floor, you’re wasting him. But you let him do a lot of what the point guard stuff entails. But then also defensively you don’t bother guarding him on the little guy. Put him on maybe the three man or even sometimes the four man if he’s a step-out player. And now you have a guy like Larry Bird who anticipates. He gets a lot of deflections and steals. He’s long, he blocks shots. And then when he gets a defensive rebound, you got a fast-break started already."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://aol.sportingnews.com/ncaa-basketball/story/2011-10-05/bob-hurley-prospect-kyle-anderson-a-magic-bird-combo

==Personal life==
Anderson is the son of Kyle Sr. and Suzanne Anderson. His grandfather, Clifton Anderson, played [[college football]] at [[Indiana Hoosiers football|Indiana]] and had a two-year professional career in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) with the [[Chicago Cardinals]] in 1952 and the [[New York Giants]] in 1953.<ref name=uclabio/> Anderson's maternal grandmother grew up in Jamaica; her father was Chinese and married a Jamaican, and they lived in Jamaica among the Chinese-Jamaicans.<ref>{{cite news|last=Zagoria|first=Adam|title=Like Jeremy Lin, UCLA-Bound Anderson Has Asian Heritage|date=February 18, 2012|work=zagsblog.com|url=http://zagsblog.com/articles/like-jeremy-lin-ucla-bound-anderson-has-asian-heritage/|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/6OB6mzU5c|archivedate=March 18, 2014|deadurl=no}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Wharton|first=David|title=Not only do Bruins visit attractions in China, they become one|date=August 23, 2012|newspaper=Los Angeles Times|url=http://articles.latimes.com/2012/aug/23/sports/la-sp-0824-ucla-basketball-china-20120824|archiveurl=http://www.webcitation.org/6OB6ubEHO|archivedate=March 18, 2014|deadurl=no}}</ref>
